paragraphs.text: # RemoteDSH
English | 中文
Remote session bridging for DSH. One machine runs as a **server** and exposes its session records re
ad-only; another runs as a **client**, connects to it, and **mirrors those remote sessions into its
own Workspace as ordinary sessions** — no custom UI is written. The sidebar, session list, and conve
rsation view are all the native ones.
## Where to configure
**UI (recommended)**: sidebar **Plugins → Installed → View dsh-remote-bridge → Configure dsh-remote-
ommended)**: sidebar **Plugins → Installed → View dsh-remote-bridge → Configure dsh-remote-bridge**.
The page edits the run mode, the server switch / listen address / port / machine name / token / pass
word / visible sessions / working-directory scope, and the client switch plus the remote list (add,
edit, remove id, label, address, token). Saving writes to `$DSH_HOME/profiles/web/cordis.patch.yml`
and reports that a restart — or toggling the plugin off and on — applies it.
**File**: the `config` of the `remote-bridge` row in `$DSH_HOME/profiles/web/cordis.patch.yml`; its
fields mirror the form one-to-one.
> The form projects only the fields a plugin declares `.volatile()`, and this plugin marks all of th

em, so the `mode`, `server`, and `client` subtrees are all editable.
> If a higher-precedence layer
(a `--patch` overlay or a home patch) overrides the same row, saving is refused with `overridden by
a home patch or command-line overlay` — edit that layer instead.
| What | Field | Notes |

| Listen address | `server.host` | `0.0.0.0` exposes the LAN; `127.0.0.1` keeps it local |
| Listen

port | `server.port` | defaults to `4590` |
| Advertised machine name | `server.name` | shown to cli

ents as “on \<name\>”; defaults to the hostname |
| Server authentication | `server.auth.token` / `s

erver.auth.password` | empty disables the check (a warning is logged) |
| Remote to connect | `clien

t.remotes[].url` | `http://<ip>:<port>`, `ws://<ip>:<port>`, or `<host>:<port>` |
| Client credentia

ls | `client.remotes[].token` / `password` | must match the server |
| Client-side label | `client.r
emotes[].label` | Workspace title prefix, e.g. “Office” |
Reload the plugin (or restart DSH) to apply.
## Connection monitor (server side)
At the top of the same configuration page sits a **Connection monitor** that refreshes every 5 secon
the top of the same configuration page sits a **Connection monitor** that refreshes every 5 seconds:
- **Inbound peers**: machine name, source IP:port, authenticated identity, client and protocol versi
ons, visible session count, connect time, duration, last activity, history-read count, and a **Disco

nnect** button.
[该节后续省略]
## Protocol and capability negotiation
The handshake reports what each side supports, and the server enables only the **intersection**:
[代码示例省略，未执行]
`welcome` answers in the same shape: `features` (negotiated), `featuresSupported` (the server's full
set), and `relays` (readable sharers with their session lists).
| Capability | Meaning |
| `sessions.read` / `history.read` | baseline reads (always present; declared so a future build can

drop one) |
| `relay.publish` | this side may publish sessions as a sharer |
| `relay.refresh` | re-

announce on a permission change, and re-announce on request (`relay/pull`) |
| `relay.subscribe` | t
his side may read what others share, and may ask for a re-pull (`relay/sync`) |
Version check: the server accepts v1–v3. A mismatch answers `protocol-mismatch` with the server's ow
n capability list, and a client also recognises a server that is too old. A v1 client has no `featur
es` field, so negotiation yields the empty set — it simply never receives relay capabilities, while
baseline reading keeps working. A peer without `relay.refresh` still works; a permission change just
takes up to one poll cycle to spread.
`GET /` reports `protocol`, `minProtocol`, `features`, and `relay` as well.
## How it works
1. A client opens `/ws` on the remote and sends `hello` (protocol version, token/password, capabilit

y set, share intent).
2. The server validates it and answers `welcome` (machine name, negotiated cap

abilities, readable sharers, session summaries), then pushes `sessions` and `event` frames.
3. The c
lient creates `$DSH_HOME/remote-bridge/<id>` per machine and registers it as a Workspace, titled e.g

. `Office (on PC-01)`.
4. Each remote session materialises as a local session (id `session-rb-<hash>

`, cwd pointing at that directory); its full log is written locally and attached to the Workspace.
5
. The mirror rides a **live Session**: events enter the in-memory session, the native `session/follo
w` pushes them to open pages, and projections (title, metadata) are folded by the native registry —

so neither the sidebar title nor live updates are implemented by this plugin.
6. The plugin also hol
ds the persistence write handle for that session, so this machine **cannot resume it** — `session/pr
ompt`, `session/rename` and friends return `session/writer-held`. The mirror is read-only by constru

ction.
7. New remote events are appended to the local log and the in-memory session; after a reconne

ct the client catches up by cursor.
8. With relay on: a sharer pushes `publish` (the catalogue it fi
ltered itself), the server re-checks the scope and broadcasts `relay/sessions`; when a reader issues
`history` with `peer`, the server forwards it to the sharer, which answers `history` with `events`,
and the server returns it to the reader. Live events travel `publish/event` → `relay/event`.
## Known limitations
- **Read-only**: the plugin holds the write handle, so this machine cannot resume or rename a mirror

(`session/writer-held`).
- **Empty sessions are hidden**: a remote session that has not started yet

is hidden by the native list, matching local behaviour.
- **fork/seed sessions degrade**: a log tha
t cannot be replayed live falls back to a pure persistence mirror, with its title restored from the

projection cache.
- **Both ends must be compatible**: the protocol is tied to the local session form

at; relay requires both ends to be ≥ 0.5.0.
- **Mirrors take disk space**: mirrored sessions are wri

tten into the local session store.
- **One writer per session**: a given remote session should be mi

rrored by one client only; two mirrors of the same id fail on the write lock.
- **Relay needs the sh
arer online**: when a sharer disconnects its sessions vanish from readers immediately (the server pu

shes `gone`), and history requests answer `relay-offline`.
- **Relay is read-only**: a reader holds
a mirror, cannot resume it, and never sends events back to the sharer.
